title: Five trades
hookLine: lay followers avoid trading in weapons, living beings, meat, intoxicants and poisons (AN 5.177)

cards: Your money is busy right now, while you're sitting here. The coffee you bought this morning, the bank holding your paycheck, the retirement fund you haven't looked at since the day you signed up.
Each one is quietly paying for something, somewhere, and most of us have no idea what. The Buddha's world had no index funds.
But it had markets, caravans and merchants, and he named five things a lay follower shouldn't trade in.

teach.b: In the Numbered Discourses, the sutta is only a few lines long. A lay follower, the Buddha says, should not engage in five kinds of trade: trade in weapons, in living beings, in meat, in intoxicants, and in poisons.
That's nearly the whole text. The old commentary fills in some meaning. Living beings, it says, means people: buying and selling human beings.
Meat means raising and selling animals for slaughter.
All five share a shape: the goods themselves are made to harm, to kill, to enslave, or to cloud the mind. Notice who it's addressed to.
Not monks; they don't trade at all. This is for householders with shops and caravans. It doesn't say commerce is wrong.
Elsewhere the Buddha describes a shopkeeper who is shrewd, capable and trustworthy, and says he soon grows rich. It draws a line around five kinds of goods.

It also doesn't settle whether to eat meat; Buddhist communities differ on that, and this sutta is about the trade. Buddhists today read it in different ways. Some read it narrowly, as a list of businesses to stay out of.
Others widen it into a question about everything their money touches: what their savings fund, what their spending supports.
The sutta itself doesn't say how wide to read it.
But the question it plants is plain: what does your money do when you're not watching? Look back at the week. Intention is the act.
As you sow. Not everything is kamma. The acrobat's balance.
A gift to everyone. Earn clean. And today, what your money does.

how: Many lay Buddhists avoid work in the five trades, and some extend the principle to how they invest and spend; teachers often cite this sutta when discussing right livelihood.

o: cloth, grain, horses, timber and pottery
weapons, living beings, meat, intoxicants, poisons
gold, silver, silk, spices and salt

games.q: the five trades: tap the pairs.

s: AN 5.177 says business is wrong for Buddhists
it names five kinds of goods; elsewhere the Buddha describes a shrewd, capable, trustworthy shopkeeper who soon grows rich.
in the commentary, trade in living beings means buying and selling people
the commentary explains it as trade in human beings.
the sutta tells monks which trades to avoid
it's addressed to lay followers; monks don't trade at all.

games.q: you're a merchant with a caravan in the Buddha's day. a buyer offers a fortune for a wagonload of swords. what does AN 5.177 say?
o: a lay follower doesn't trade in weapons.
sell, but give the profit away.
games.why: weapons are the first of the five trades the Buddha says a lay follower should not engage in.

practice: Think of the last three things you paid for, and follow each one back a step: who made it, who sold it, where the money went next.
You won't know everything, and that's fine; just notice the trail, and how rarely anyone looks at it. Then rest with the breath, and let a quiet question sit there: what would I want my money to do?

wordCard.voice: Five trades. Weapons, living beings, meat, intoxicants and poisons: the five a lay follower doesn't trade in, from the book of fives.

orig.note: Pali vaṇijjā: trade, commerce, the word AN 5.177 uses for the five.

carryVoice: Your line: what your money does. The sutta leaves it to you how wide to read it. That's the week.
